title: Like No Business I Know

jokes.text: Staff watching Leno react to Bobcat: 'You can tell Leno's pissed. Look at him. That bobcat has got serious mental problems.' / 'I think he's got incredible balls.' / 'Paula, don't say balls. Men find that off-putting.' / 'Thanks for the tip.' / 'Don't say tip.'
jokes.setup: Paula says Bobcat has 'incredible balls' in admiration
jokes.punchline: Larry corrects her — 'men find that off-putting' — then immediately catches 'tip' as another double entendre, creating a rapid-fire running gag
jokes.explanation: The rapid-fire double-entendre escalation is extremely well-constructed. 'Men find that off-putting' is a perfectly Larry-ish bit of faux-etiquette nonsense, and catching 'tip' immediately after shows a tight comedic ear. The economy is near-perfect — four lines, two jokes, both land. Larry policing word choices while discussing a man who just burned Leno's chair is great character irony.

dialogue.line: Set his furniture on fire?
Oh, no, don't set that on fire.

jokes.text: I think he's got incredible balls. / Paula, don't say 'balls.' Men find that off-putting. / Thanks for the tip. / Don't say 'tip.'
jokes.setup: Paula praises Bobcat's audacity; Larry reflexively polices her language
jokes.punchline: The escalating word-trap: 'balls' → 'tip' → implied third step never arrived, the audience completes the joke
jokes.explanation: A beautifully tight escalating wordplay exchange. The structure is perfect: Paula walks into the word trap, Larry corrects it with smug paternalism, Paula's comeback lands the second trap, and Larry's instant 'don't say tip' completes the comedy circuit with perfect economy. The audience mentally supplies the third double-entendre, making them co-conspirators. One of the tightest joke constructions in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: That bobcat has got serious mental problems.

dialogue.speaker: Unknown
dialogue.line: Paula, don't say 'balls.' Men find that off-putting.

dialogue.speaker: Unknown

jokes.text: 'They're whores. Whores. Whores.' — on the Tonight Show booking Bobcat after his Arsenio stunt
jokes.setup: Artie explains that Arsenio booked Bobcat after the stunt got press, so the Tonight Show did the same
jokes.punchline: Artie delivers three-beat 'Whores. Whores. Whores.' with the flat moral authority of someone who's seen it all
jokes.explanation: Pure Artie. Rip Torn's delivery of three repetitions is the joke — it's a rhythmic, almost liturgical condemnation of showbiz. The triple repetition is structurally elegant and quintessentially Artie's worldview: he's not surprised, he's just naming what he sees. Highly quotable, totally character-specific.

dialogue.line: They're whores. Whores. Whores.

jokes.text: Bobcat here yet? Yes. Good. Michael Bolton and Regis Philbin are here as well.
jokes.setup: Larry asks about his most dangerous guest
jokes.punchline: The casual equivalence of Bobcat (who just set a chair on fire nationally) with Michael Bolton and Regis Philbin as a list of 'guests who are here' — the absurdity of show business normalcy
jokes.explanation: The comedic value is in the deadpan juxtaposition — treating Bobcat's arrival the same as Regis and Bolton. Functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: if I wanted to see furniture destroyed or our set ablaze, I'd go over to Jimmy Caan's place

jokes.text: Artie warns Bobcat about 'crazy stuff': 'He'll be zany and wacky, and the set will remain completely intact.'
jokes.setup: Larry asks if Artie told Bobcat no crazy stuff
jokes.punchline: Artie's assurance is itself darkly sarcastic — 'zany and wacky' paired with 'completely intact' signals he doesn't believe a word of it
jokes.explanation: Artie knows chaos is coming and manages it with wry detachment. Rewatch bonus because we know the set does NOT remain intact. The irony is present but requires you to hear it in Torn's voice to fully land.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I get the spring right up my ass

jokes.text: 'If I wanted to see furniture destroyed or our set ablaze, I'd go over to Jimmy Caan's place.'
jokes.setup: Larry says he likes pranky stunts but has limits
jokes.punchline: The casual celebrity name-drop implying Jimmy Caan routinely destroys furniture at home — a specific, insider-Hollywood joke
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'Jimmy Caan's place' elevates what could be a throwaway line. It's an insider showbiz joke — Caan's reputation for volatility — delivered with the casual authority of someone who actually moves in those circles. Very Larry Sanders in tone: name-dropping as both humor and status signal.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: My ass is my fortune

jokes.text: 'It was right in the middle of Helen Hunt last night, I get the spring right up my ass.'
jokes.setup: Larry is examining a broken guest chair, poking at something in the cushion
jokes.punchline: He reveals the spring jabbed him during a guest interview — the mundane indignity of a broken TV set chair disrupting a celebrity interview
jokes.explanation: The juxtaposition of the glamour of a TV talk show with a broken chair stabbing the host mid-interview is very on-brand for this show's deflation of showbiz. 'Right in the middle of Helen Hunt' is perfectly placed — the celebrity name makes the mundane indignity funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Hey, now.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: It's the same as its always been.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: No, no, I don't think so... hey, now!

jokes.text: 'Thank you. My ass is my fortune.'
jokes.setup: Larry has just had a spring fixed in the guest chair that was jabbing his rear
jokes.punchline: He thanks the crew and delivers 'My ass is my fortune' with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: Four words, maximum absurdity, delivered deadpan. The joke works on multiple levels: it's literally true (his performance is his livelihood and he's protecting his physical comfort), but the phrasing is hilariously pompous. It's perfectly Larry — self-important to a comic degree. Economy score near-perfect. Highly quotable out of context.

dialogue.speaker: Regis
dialogue.line: Look out! Who's that big stud in the mustache? Uh-oh! Hey! Uh-oh!

jokes.text: Hank testing his microphone, narrating his own echo: 'Hey, now. / Hey, now! / Look out! Who's that big stud in the mustache? / Uh-oh! Hey! / Uh-oh! How are ya, hanker?'
jokes.setup: Hank is supposedly testing his mic for reverb issues
jokes.punchline: He turns the mic test into a self-admiring one-man show, talking to himself as if greeting a celebrity — who is himself
jokes.explanation: Classic Hank — the professional task (mic test) is immediately subverted into a vehicle for self-aggrandizement. He greets himself as a stud in a mustache. The character specificity is high; no one but Hank would do this. Tambor's delivery would sell it completely.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: the wife's been on my ass a little bit about the snacks. I put the crackers out in the garage, and something got into that box and built a nest

jokes.text: Hank tells Regis he put the gifted crackers in the garage and 'something got into that box and built a nest.'
jokes.setup: Regis asks if Hank got the case of crackers they sent as a gift from their commercial
jokes.punchline: Hank buried the lead — they're not displayed proudly, they're in the garage where something nested in them
jokes.explanation: There's something very real about this — Hank is trying to be gracious but the truth escapes him. 'Something got into that box and built a nest' is the kind of detail that feels observed from life. The awkwardness of the social situation (someone sent you a gift that ended up as rodent housing) is mined well.

dialogue.speaker: Regis
dialogue.line: I'm the luckiest man in show business, or, uh... everyone says so. I have to agree.

jokes.text: Hank's response to being offered the sidekick job: 'Well, that is, uh... that is, um... that's an honor. I'm, um... I'm honored and I'm deeply... I'm honored.'
jokes.setup: Regis has just offered Hank a sidekick position on his new network show
jokes.punchline: Hank's response collapses into a loop of 'honored' — he can't get past the word, visibly processing the implications while performing gratitude
jokes.explanation: Tambor is a master of this kind of verbal paralysis. The joke is entirely in the looping of 'honored' — it's not funny because of what he says but because of what he can't say. He's clearly torn and stunned, performing graciousness while his brain scrambles. High character integration because only Hank — the perpetually under-confident sidekick — would respond to a promotion offer this way.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: What would say? / I'd say that's great! That's great!

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Well, who's the lucky cable channel?

dialogue.speaker: Regis
dialogue.line: No! No cable, no, no. Network.

jokes.text: Hank turns down the sidekick offer with great dignity: 'I'm gonna turn you down. Because there's a loyalty to this place. These people are like my family.' — then immediately adds 'Darlene? Darlene, can you hear me? Call Margaret! Tell her I'm 2 to 4 minutes late!'
jokes.setup: Hank delivers a moving, principled speech about loyalty and family — his people, his home
jokes.punchline: The speech is immediately undercut when he shouts for his assistant to call his wife because he's minutes late — revealing the decision is his wife's, not his principled stand
jokes.explanation: This is a standout structural joke. Hank's 'loyalty' speech is genuinely moving for about three seconds — and then the curtain falls and we see Margaret is pulling the strings. The juxtaposition is near-perfect: the gravity of 'these people are like my family' against the panic of 'tell her I'm 2 to 4 minutes late.' The '2 to 4 minutes' specificity is a great detail — very Hank, hedging even with his wife. High character integration and structure scores are well-earned.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Get outta here, Regis Philbin

jokes.text: Bobcat explaining the Leno chair fire: 'I actually soaked the thing... I actually burned my ass. I got a couple welts on it... I don't want to toot my own horn, but I was pretty proud that I could actually get a couple jokes off while this was going on.'
jokes.setup: Bobcat is recounting exactly how he set Leno's chair on fire
jokes.punchline: He burned his own ass in the process, got welts, and is still proud of his comedic timing through the pain — the professional dedication is absurd
jokes.explanation: 'I don't want to toot my own horn, but I was pretty proud' is a great Bobcat-specific detail — the professional comic's ego applied to arson. The self-effacing opener followed by genuine pride in chaos is perfectly in character. Bobcat Goldthwait as himself is doing character comedy in the purest sense.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Wow. Well, that is, uh... that is, um... that's an honor. I'm, um... I'm honored and I'm deeply... I'm honored.

jokes.text: Larry on Bobcat's legal situation: 'Hey, then we don't have to do it' — and Bobcat's lawyer told him to shut up because 'I keep making it worse.'
jokes.setup: Larry suggests talking about the Leno incident on air; Bobcat says his lawyer told him to stop discussing it
jokes.punchline: 'I keep talking about it, and it's just not good' — deadpan admission of his own inability to shut up
jokes.explanation: A functional comedy beat — the guilty party who legally can't discuss something but clearly wants to and keeps making it worse. Bobcat's self-awareness about his own lack of restraint is in character. Competent but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: My wife Margaret. She gets mad when I'm... I'm late. She doesn't get mad, she gets, uh, upset... concerned!

jokes.text: Robert le chat, in person!
jokes.setup: Artie greets Bobcat Goldthwait backstage
jokes.punchline: Artie using the French translation of 'Goldthwait' (chat = cat) as a mock-formal greeting — both a joke and an establishment of hierarchy (Artie isn't intimidated by this wild card)
jokes.explanation: This is a Rip Torn specialty — the slightly arcane put-down that asserts intellectual dominance. Artie translating Goldthwait into French while calling it 'le chat' is both clever wordplay and a power move. It's Artie saying 'I've already figured you out, kid.'

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Call Margaret! Tell her I'm 2 to 4 minutes late!

jokes.text: Artie to Bobcat: 'I just love your clown movie. I'm just a sucker for drunk clowns.'
jokes.setup: Artie greets Bobcat warmly and mentions being a fan
jokes.punchline: 'I'm just a sucker for drunk clowns' — delivered with complete earnestness by a man who clearly means it
jokes.explanation: Only Artie would express genuine, sincere appreciation for 'drunk clowns' as a genre. It's oddly specific and completely believable coming from Torn's character. The economy is excellent — it tells you everything about Artie's aesthetic in five words.

dialogue.speaker: Bobcat
dialogue.line: I actually burned my ass. I got a couple welts on it from it.

jokes.text: Artie's 'welcome speech' to Bobcat: 'That fabric on the guest chair is no longer being manufactured... those huge Larry letters over by the band, they're much more expensive than they look. And don't get near my fucking plants.'
jokes.setup: Artie begins what seems like a straightforward list of things Bobcat shouldn't damage on the set
jokes.punchline: It escalates to 'don't get near my fucking plants' — the personal, possessive fury of a man whose plants are his emotional anchor
jokes.explanation: This is excellent character comedy. The escalation from professional concerns (chair fabric, set pieces) to intensely personal ('my fucking plants... they're my babies') reveals something genuine about Artie — underneath the ruthless producer is a man who has chosen plants as the thing he will protect. The profanity lands because it's proportionate to how much he cares. Then 'See you on television!' as a cheery sign-off is a perfect button.

dialogue.speaker: Bobcat
dialogue.line: I don't want to toot my own horn, but I was pretty proud that I could actually get a couple jokes off while this was going on

jokes.text: 'They're my babies. See you on television!'
jokes.setup: Artie has just delivered his threatening speech about his plants
jokes.punchline: He pivots immediately to a cheerful showbiz send-off — 'See you on television!' — as if the threat never happened
jokes.explanation: The tonal whiplash from 'my babies' to 'See you on television!' is the joke. It's a perfect button on the previous beat — Artie threatening a guest and then performing the industry-standard warm send-off as if he didn't just threaten him. The contrast between the two registers is what makes it land.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: I just love your clown movie. I'm just a sucker for drunk clowns.

jokes.text: Hank's agent Sidney enters to a song Hank is singing: '♪ it is Sidney, it is Sidney ♪ / ♪ it is Sid ♪ / ♪ it's the agent who's been with me a long time / who's sitting on the couch... ♪' then Sidney: 'Hank, please, I'm your agent, not your mother.' Hank: 'You are... you are my mother? All right, I'm your mother.'
jokes.setup: Sidney arrives; Hank greets him by breaking into an improvised celebratory song
jokes.punchline: Sidney cuts him off, denying he's Hank's mother; Hank immediately processes this as a confirmation and accepts it
jokes.explanation: Hank's relationship with his agent as a maternal figure is revealed in a burst of absurdist musical comedy. The song itself is funny in its earnestness — Hank improvises on the fly and it's terrible in a charming way. The mother confusion is a bit loose but Tambor's commitment sells it. Shows the depth of Hank's neediness.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: don't get near my fucking plants. They're my babies.

jokes.text: Jesus Christ. Ho!
jokes.setup: Bobcat has just received Artie's threatening welcome speech
jokes.punchline: Bobcat's stunned reaction — the man who set a chair on fire on national television is rattled by an old man's plant speech
jokes.explanation: The reaction beat works well in context — Bobcat (the chaos agent) being genuinely rattled by Artie (the authority figure) is good comedy. But as a transcribed line it's mostly a setup for the previous joke's impact.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Jesus Christ. Ho! ♪ it is Sidney, it is Sidney ♪

jokes.text: Hank floats his plan: 'Live with Hank and Kathie Lee.'
jokes.setup: Hank explains that if Regis leaves the morning show, there's a vacancy — and begins pitching himself as a replacement
jokes.punchline: 'Live with Hank and Kathie Lee' — the absurdity of this sidekick imagining himself as a morning show host replacing Regis, paired with Kathie Lee
jokes.explanation: The joke is entirely in the specificity of the casting and the grandiosity of Hank's self-image. 'Live with Hank and Kathie Lee' is funny because it's almost plausible — and yet completely implausible for Hank. Sidney's silent horror is the rest of the joke. Five words that crystallize Hank's delusional ambition.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: You are... you are my mother?

dialogue.speaker: Sid
dialogue.line: All right, I'm your mother.

jokes.text: Sidney: 'Hank-eleh. Chach-keleh. This is not a smart move. Here. The Larry Sanders show. This is your base. Where did you come up with such a farkuckt idea?'
jokes.setup: Sidney processes Hank's 'Live with Hank and Kathie Lee' pitch
jokes.punchline: 'Where did you come up with such a farkuckt idea?' — delivered with the exhausted Yiddish wisdom of a man who has managed Hank for too long
jokes.explanation: The Yiddish diminutives ('Hank-eleh,' 'Chach-keleh,' 'farkuckt') are a beautiful character choice for Sidney — they signal warmth and condescension simultaneously. Only this specific agent-client dynamic could produce this line. 'This is your base' — pointing at the show — is a lovely touch of industry-insider realism.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Live with Hank and Kathie Lee

jokes.text: Sidney: 'The last time I had lunch with my wife I ended up redoing the living room in a pattern that I'm not allowed to sit down on.'
jokes.setup: Hank mentions the idea came from lunch with his wife; Sidney warns this is a red flag
jokes.punchline: Sidney's own wife-lunch anecdote: a living room redecoration so precious he's banned from sitting on his own furniture
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes. The detail is perfect: not just that lunch with the wife has consequences, but that the specific consequence is furniture you're 'not allowed to sit down on.' The absurdity escalates naturally — a living room redone, then the kicker that it's too precious to use. It captures the specific emasculation of marriage with economical, quotable precision. Could stand alone as a joke in any context. Genuinely exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Sid
dialogue.line: Hank-eleh. Chach-keleh. This is not a smart move.

jokes.text: Hank on phone with Margaret, tells Sidney 'Can I have a little privacy, please?' Sidney: 'You realize I'll have to get up?' — then the sound of him struggling to rise, followed by a crash and 'Just a mild concussion. Don't worry yourself. Please?'
jokes.setup: Hank asks Sidney for privacy during his wife's call; Sidney points out he'll have to physically get up
jokes.punchline: Sidney's exit results in a crash and a stoically delivered 'Just a mild concussion. Don't worry yourself.'
jokes.explanation: The slapstick is perfectly deployed here — Sidney's protest about having to get up primes us, the crash confirms it, and then 'Just a mild concussion. Don't worry yourself. Please?' is a beautiful deadpan button. The 'Please?' is the killer — injured and still performing politeness. This is character comedy through physical action.

dialogue.speaker: Sid
dialogue.line: The last time I had lunch with my wife I ended up redoing the living room in a pattern that I'm not allowed to sit down on

jokes.text: He's leaving now. Yeah. No, he's doing his leaving thing. Yeah. Ooh! Just a mild concussion. Don't worry yourself. Please?
jokes.setup: Hank has asked Sid to leave; Hank is narrating Sid's exit to Margaret on the phone
jokes.punchline: Sid apparently walks into something or bumps himself on the way out, and Hank's response is 'just a mild concussion, don't worry yourself' — the casualness of reporting a possible head injury as minor inconvenience
jokes.explanation: The visual gag of Sid bumping into something is funny, but the real joke is Hank's narration: 'just a mild concussion, don't worry yourself' — delivered with the same level of concern he'd apply to spilled coffee. The 'Please?' on the end (to Margaret) is perfect — he's already moved on. Strong economy.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Just a mild concussion. Don't worry yourself. Please?

jokes.text: Artie on Hank's intellectual limitations: 'Not enough oxygen to the brain as a fetus, that's my first guess.'
jokes.setup: Larry asks what's wrong with Hank this time
jokes.punchline: Artie attributes Hank's behavior to prenatal oxygen deprivation — a devastating dismissal delivered as if it's a medical opinion
jokes.explanation: Rip Torn's deadpan authority turns this into something special. 'That's my first guess' implies there are other guesses and they're all equally clinical and devastating. It's a perfectly calibrated insult — specific enough to be funny, delivered with enough detachment to not seem mean-spirited. Pure Artie.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: not enough oxygen to the brain as a fetus, that's my first guess.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: That would be mine.

jokes.text: Larry: 'That's my guess too.' — following Artie's fetus oxygen diagnosis
jokes.setup: Artie diagnoses Hank with prenatal oxygen deprivation
jokes.punchline: Larry agrees instantly, confirming this is a shared and settled understanding between them
jokes.explanation: A short agreement beat that extends the previous joke. Works because it confirms the diagnosis as institutional knowledge rather than one man's opinion. The brevity is its virtue.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: What happened?

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: He married her.

jokes.text: Artie on Hank's wife situation: 'His wife is pursuing it.' — after Larry asks if Hank is pursuing the Regis sidekick offer
jokes.setup: Larry asks if Hank is actively pursuing the Regis sidekick offer
jokes.punchline: 'His wife is pursuing it' — three words that replace Hank's agency entirely
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy. Three words that say everything: Hank has no agency, Margaret is the engine of this subplot, and everyone in the office knows it. Artie's flat delivery would make this even funnier. One of the most quotable lines in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Well, I'd like to know what we're talking about before I do that.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Don't worry about it. Take a chair. Just a man-to-man chat.

jokes.text: Larry: 'Don't you want me to tell you how I handle it?' Artie: 'No, just handle it.' Larry: 'That's enough for you?' Artie: 'Yeah, it's more than enough for me just to know that you're handling it.'
jokes.setup: Larry offers to explain his plan for dealing with the Hank situation
jokes.punchline: Artie refuses any details — his faith in the process over the specifics is total, and the exchange reveals Larry's need for validation and Artie's complete indifference to it
jokes.explanation: This exchange reveals the dynamic between Larry and Artie perfectly — Larry needs approval and explanation; Artie trusts results over process. 'It's more than enough for me just to know that you're handling it' is a great line that could read as faith or as a complete dismissal of Larry's need to explain himself.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: You got some action, huh? You finally bagged that chick at NBC, right?

jokes.text: On Hank's wife Margaret: 'I thought she was really quiet and sweet.' 'She was.' 'What happened?' 'He married her.'
jokes.setup: Larry wonders how Margaret transformed from 'quiet and sweet' to an ambitious force driving Hank's career moves
jokes.punchline: 'He married her.' — Artie's explanation is that marriage itself is the transformative agent
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best pure joke. It's structurally perfect — four lines, a four-word answer that reframes the entire question. 'He married her' implies that marriage inevitably changes people, with marriage itself as the cause of transformation rather than any individual's fault. It's dark, observational, economical, and devastatingly quotable. The structure is classical setup/punchline but the punchline is genuinely witty. This is what Artie as a character is for — delivering the truth with minimum words. One of the best lines in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: People always have told me everything all my life. I can't help that.

jokes.text: Larry: 'Make him pretty, Bruno.' — transitioning to hair/makeup
jokes.setup: Larry finishes the Hank discussion and heads to his own prep
jokes.punchline: 'Make him pretty' is the slightly narcissistic, slightly self-deprecating way he refers to his own cosmetic prep
jokes.explanation: A minor transition beat with mild character flavor. 'Make him pretty' referring to himself is a vanity tell, but it's not a strong joke on its own — more of a texture moment that reveals Larry's self-regard.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: If I was pussy-whipped, you'd be talking to me the way I'm talking to you now.

jokes.text: Hank won't close the door to Larry's office without knowing what they're discussing: 'Well, I'd like to know what we're talking about before I do that.'
jokes.setup: Larry asks Hank to close the door for a private man-to-man chat
jokes.punchline: Hank refuses to close the door without knowing the topic first — a paranoid defense mechanism disguised as reasonableness
jokes.explanation: Pure Hank — the anxiety of not knowing what's coming makes him refuse even a trivial gesture (closing a door). It's a small, beautifully character-specific moment that sets up the tension of the scene while being funny in itself. The comedy is entirely in the character.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: She looks at you like she's got X-ray vision. Gives me the creeps.

jokes.text: Hank guesses the reason for the closed-door meeting: 'I know what's up. You got some action, huh? You finally bagged that chick at NBC, right?'
jokes.setup: Larry is trying to have a serious conversation about the Regis offer
jokes.punchline: Hank's mind goes immediately to sexual conquest, assuming the secret meeting is to share an affair victory
jokes.explanation: Hank's first guess about the secret meeting is a sex victory — this says volumes about Hank's priorities and his understanding of male bonding. The specificity of 'that chick at NBC' implies an ongoing subplot we're not privy to, which gives the joke a real-world texture. Good character misdirection.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: that is a severe astigmatism, OK?

jokes.text: Larry reveals he knows about Regis; Hank: 'Aw, cut the crap, Hank' — Larry calls himself Hank by mistake in the confrontation
jokes.setup: Larry confronts Hank about the Regis offer
jokes.punchline: Larry says 'Aw, cut the crap, Hank' — calling Hank by his own name as if Larry momentarily lost track of which person he is in the conversation
jokes.explanation: A small self-referential slip — Larry trying to be forceful and confusing whose name he's using. Works as a moment of Larry's frazzled authority. Minor but charming.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I can't allow her to lift her skirt for every other show that comes along!

jokes.text: People always have told me everything all my life. I can't help that.
jokes.setup: Larry asks who told him about Regis; Hank deflects
jokes.punchline: Hank framing his information-gathering as a passive, God-given gift — 'people always tell me everything, I can't help it' — as if he's not actively gossiping and scheming
jokes.explanation: Hank reframing his gossiping as an involuntary spiritual gift is excellent character comedy. The 'I can't help that' as if he's cursed with universal trust is perfectly delivered irony.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I quit.

jokes.text: Larry on Hank's wife: 'If I was pussy-whipped, you'd be talking to me the way I'm talking to you now.'
jokes.setup: Larry accuses Hank of being controlled by Margaret
jokes.punchline: Larry frames his confrontational, aggressive manner as what he would do 'if he were pussy-whipped' — implying this is the opposite, while we see the irony that the 'non-whipped' guy is also afraid of his guest relationships
jokes.explanation: Larry sets up a comparison that positions himself as the liberated one, but we know Larry is controlled by his own anxieties about ratings, guests, and approval. The show earns the irony without underlining it. Good character work.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: You do not apply the term 'pussy whipped' to Hank Kingsley. No? No. He has never been, nor never will be whipped by anything let alone a pussy.

jokes.text: Artie on Margaret: 'She looks at you like she's got X-ray vision. Gives me the creeps.' And: 'I never liked Margaret.'
jokes.setup: Artie is explaining why he believes Margaret controls Hank
jokes.punchline: 'She looks at you like she's got X-ray vision. Gives me the creeps.' — Artie delivers a specific, visual metaphor that reveals even he is a little afraid of her
jokes.explanation: The X-ray vision metaphor is original and specific — it's not just that she's perceptive, she sees through you. Even the grizzled, unflappable Artie is creeped out by her, which elevates Margaret as a comic threat. 'I never liked Margaret' delivered flatly before the elaboration is a great ordering choice.

dialogue.line: Margaret called. She says it's urgent.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: See that? Yeah, I'm really pussy whipped. She call from home or the car?

dialogue.line: Home.

jokes.text: Hank defends Margaret's penetrating stare: 'That is a severe astigmatism, OK?'
jokes.setup: Artie says Margaret looks at people like she has X-ray vision, which gives him the creeps
jokes.punchline: Hank's defense of his wife is that her unsettling gaze is merely a medical eye condition
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional. The joke works on multiple levels: Hank is defending his wife against a supernatural characterization with a mundane medical explanation, but the specificity of 'severe astigmatism' is perfect — it's exactly the kind of detail Hank would deploy as if it settled the argument. It also simultaneously confirms Artie's point (the stare is unusual enough to warrant explanation) while denying it. The callback structure is flawless. One of the episode's best lines.

jokes.text: Artie: 'I'm sorry. Don't get me wrong — she's a lovely girl. But I can't allow her to lift her skirt for every other show that comes along.'

jokes.punchline: 'I can't allow her to lift her skirt for every other show that comes along' — mixing up agency (it's Hank, not Margaret, being offered jobs) with a gendered idiom applied to the wrong person
jokes.explanation: Artie's mixed metaphor is funny because it's genuinely confused — he's saying Margaret is peddling Hank like a commodity, but the phrasing ('lift her skirt') applies to Margaret and makes no literal sense, which is exactly the kind of old-school, slightly archaic expression Artie would use. It's also Artie taking ownership of Hank's career as his charge.

jokes.explanation: Artie's refusal to be deterred by Hank quitting is great character comedy — he genuinely seems to believe the situation is improved. 'I tried to help' when what he did was call Hank's wife a whore is a marvelous piece of self-justification.

jokes.punchline: 'Hasta la vista, baby' as Hank's dramatic exit line — a Terminator 2 reference used as a self-styled power move by a deeply unempowered man in the middle of a crumbling negotiation.
jokes.explanation: The Terminator reference is dated-intentionally — Hank reaches for cultural currency and it's slightly embarrassing. But the contrast between the movie's cool delivery and Hank's flustered situation makes it work. The 'I'm a pro' speech preceding it is the setup.

jokes.text: Hank: 'You do not apply the term pussy-whipped to Hank Kingsley. No? No. He has never been, nor never will be whipped by anything, let alone a pussy.'
jokes.setup: Hank, having quit, delivers a formal defense of his dignity referring to himself in the third person
jokes.punchline: The third-person self-defense is pompous and funny; the phrase 'whipped by anything, let alone a pussy' is both the defense and its own undermining — as he's about to answer a call from his wife
jokes.explanation: Hank speaking in the third person to defend himself is peak Hank Kingsley — it's how a man who sees himself as a public figure defends his honor. And the irony that he's defending himself as someone who has never been 'whipped' right before taking a call from his wife is the show's architecture at its best. The formal register ('He has never been, nor never will be') against the subject matter is a great comedic contrast.

jokes.text: Hank gets the call: Margaret is on line 4. Hank: 'Yeah, like I give a shit.' — then immediately asks 'She call from home or the car?'
jokes.setup: Hank has just declared he is not whipped and doesn't care about his wife's calls
jokes.punchline: He immediately betrays his indifference by needing to know which location she's calling from — a tell that he's tracking her movements
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's comedic masterpiece. The construction is flawless: Hank declares independence ('like I give a shit'), and the punchline — 'She call from home or the car?' — arrives three seconds later and detonates everything he just said. The question reveals he is absolutely tracking her movements, that her location matters for some tactical reason, and that 'giving a shit' is an understatement. The structural gap between the bravado and the surrender is perfect. This is what a 9 looks like.

The timing is everything, and the show earns it completely. 'She says it's urgent' is the perfect wording — not just a call, but URGENT. This is a textbook ironic callback that functions as the punctuation mark on the entire scene.

jokes.punchline: Bobcat, reading the energy, offers to show Hank 'something really kooky' if he asks again — a veiled threat that becomes a comedic confrontation
jokes.explanation: The situational irony is rich: Hank, who is at his most pussy-whipped, asks Bobcat about 'his lady' and gets the response of a genuinely dangerous person. The script places Hank's wife problems directly adjacent to someone who would lose his mind over the same topic. The reaction beat (what Bobcat does to provoke 'Guy's a fucking wing nut') is the implicit punchline.

jokes.text: Kathie Lee won't work with Hank because he locked her in the trunk of a Camaro at an auto show in Buffalo in 1979.
jokes.setup: Sidney reports that Kathie Lee doesn't want to work with Hank and mentions why
jokes.punchline: The specific, detailed, absurd reason: locked in a Camaro trunk at an auto show in Buffalo in 1979 'for laughs'
jokes.explanation: The specificity is what elevates this to exceptional: not just 'auto show' but 'Buffalo'; not just 'locked in a car' but 'trunk of a Camaro'; not just 'as a prank' but 'for laughs.' Each detail is funnier than the last. It also perfectly characterizes young Hank as someone whose ideas of fun were genuinely traumatizing. The show trusts the audience to understand all the layers without underlining them.

jokes.text: She, um... she feels there'll be some difficulty. / She said that? In so many words. / What'd she say? / She doesn't want to work with you. / She said that? In so many words. / Come on, what did... she hates you! / She hates me?
jokes.setup: Sid is diplomatically reporting Kathie Lee's response to working with Hank.
jokes.punchline: The escalation from 'some difficulty' → 'she doesn't want to work with you' → 'she hates you' as Hank keeps pressing for the exact wording. Each level is funnier as the diplomacy collapses.
jokes.explanation: Classic escalation structure — the diplomatic softening that collapses under Hank's insistence on precision. The rhythm of 'in so many words' repeated twice before the dam breaks is perfectly timed. Hank's genuine surprise at 'she hates you' (she does, he's never met her) sets up the punchline.

jokes.text: Hank insists it wasn't Kathie Lee Gifford he locked in the trunk — it was Cathy Lee Crosby. 'Oh. Oh! Oh, shit. Shit! Listen, it's better... no, no.'
jokes.setup: Hank defends himself against the Kathie Lee accusation
jokes.punchline: His defense — 'That's Cathy Lee Crosby' — is immediately followed by the dawning realization that this is NOT better, followed by a cascade of 'Oh shit's
jokes.explanation: This is nearly perfect comedic escalation. Hank's clarification ('That's Cathy Lee Crosby') is meant to exonerate him but actually opens a second crime. Sidney's pause, followed by 'Oh. Oh! Oh, shit,' shows the joke landing in real time — the correction is worse than the original accusation. The escalating realization structure is classically executed. One of the episode's top moments.

jokes.text: Hank: '...so I, uh... and so I, uh... I quit.' — telling his wife he quit his job
jokes.setup: Hank is reporting to his wife (Margaret, on the phone) the events of the day, including the fight with Artie
jokes.punchline: He reveals — mid-sentence, stumbling — that he quit, the audience hearing it at the same moment Margaret does
jokes.explanation: The cringe of Hank having to tell Margaret he quit — when she's the one who pushed him toward the Regis job but he also quit the main show — is excellent situational comedy. His stumbling delivery mirrors the awkwardness of the call.

jokes.punchline: The silence is the joke — Margaret's response is apparently so devastating that Hank's next line is a panicked 'What are we gonna do?'
jokes.explanation: The implied silence of Margaret (we hear only Hank's side) is used brilliantly — her reaction is performed entirely through Hank's panicked response. 'What are we gonna do?' from a man who just delivered a speech about dignity is a great deflation.

jokes.punchline: The solution to the entire episode's crisis — 'you'd be very happy to be his sidekick' — is the job Hank already rejected while pretending to not want it. The full circle is the comedy.
jokes.explanation: The circular logic of the episode's plot crystallizes here — all of Hank's scheming and loyalty speeches return him to where he started, except now he has to go back hat in hand. Structural comedy more than joke comedy.

jokes.explanation: Sidney's pivot — from 'can you live with that?' to 'more importantly, can your wife?' — is a great character moment. He's the only person who can say what everyone else is thinking, and he says it with the matter-of-fact efficiency of a man who has seen this before.

jokes.explanation: The specificity of the plan is what makes it brilliant: not just vomit, but Denny's grand slam first (because he's a vegetarian so pork makes it special), not just vomit on Kathie Lee, but triggered by the word 'Cody.' The cultural specificity of Kathie Lee's notorious Cody references makes this an insider joke that rewards knowledge of the era. Bobcat's deadpan explanation of his detailed preparation is deeply funny.

jokes.text: Bobcat: 'But I also want to hit him, too, 'cause I don't want to be sexist.' Artie: 'And get Gelman while you're at it.' Bobcat: 'No, I don't have... I don't have that kind of range.'

jokes.explanation: This is a gem. The escalation from 'sexism' concerns (wanting to vomit on Regis too for parity) to Artie's casual suggestion to include Gelman, to Bobcat's professional assessment of his 'range' — treating projectile vomiting as a craft with technical limitations — is inspired. 'I don't have that kind of range' is one of the episode's most quotable lines. Artie's complete seriousness in engaging with the plan is perfect character work for both of them.

jokes.setup: Hank approaches Larry backstage before the show with an Important Speech.

jokes.explanation: Hank's need to verbally commit to professionalism is itself evidence of its absence. Larry's response ('Good to hear') without any of the expected emotional engagement is the quiet punchline — he just wants Hank to show up.

jokes.explanation: It's a simple line but it lands because it's accurate and because it captures the Larry-Hank dynamic perfectly. Larry's superficial warmth and Hank's need for genuine connection are the show's engine, and 'You are cold, baby' is a clean summary. Hank's wounded dignity is always good for a laugh.

jokes.explanation: A dry Larry-Artie exchange that works as an industry insider joke about the expectation (and dread) of celebrity guests breaking into song. Larry's 'I'll give him that' is perfectly delivered resignation.

jokes.text: Larry on Regis after the on-air segment: 'I was really uncomfortable. I really don't want to have Regis on again.' 'At least he didn't sing.' 'Yeah. No, I'll give him that.'
jokes.setup: Larry decompresses after the on-air Regis interview
jokes.punchline: The bar for Regis's acceptability is 'at least he didn't sing' — a very low threshold treated as a genuine concession
jokes.explanation: The backhanded praise ('at least he didn't sing') is a classic Larry deflation. Larry's discomfort with Regis trying to poach his sidekick is real, and the cattiness of the critique is very Larry. Good character texture.

jokes.text: I really don't want to have Regis on again. At least he didn't sing. / Yeah. No, I'll give him that.
jokes.setup: Post-Regis segment, Larry is debriefing with Artie about not wanting Regis back because he tried to poach Hank.
jokes.punchline: 'At least he didn't sing' as the minimal positive spin on Regis Philbin's guest appearance — the bar for success is simply not breaking into song.
jokes.explanation: The standard for Regis being 'fine' is that he refrained from singing. It works as a backhanded compliment that reveals how low the bar is. Artie's grudging concession ('I'll give him that') is perfect Artie economy.

jokes.text: Let me get my baby elephant palm off the set. I raised it from a mere nut.
jokes.setup: Artie is worried about Bobcat's upcoming segment and goes to retrieve his plant from the set
jokes.punchline: Artie's plant-parenting autobiography — 'I raised it from a mere nut' — delivered with the sincerity of a man discussing a child
jokes.explanation: The payoff on the plants running gag — Artie rushing to save his baby elephant palm before Bobcat's segment — is excellent. 'I raised it from a mere nut' has perfect gravity, treating the plant's origin story with the weight of a family narrative. High character integration.

jokes.text: Artie threatens Bobcat with his plants: 'Let me get my baby elephant palm off the set. I raised it from a mere nut.'
jokes.setup: Artie is concerned about the plant safety before Bobcat's segment
jokes.punchline: 'I raised it from a mere nut.' — The tenderness of a tough producer discussing his palm tree's origin story
jokes.explanation: The plant running gag pays off here with 'I raised it from a mere nut' — a line that reveals Artie has a genuine parental relationship with his plants. The callback to the earlier threat deepens the joke. Rip Torn's absolute sincerity about plant parentage is the source of the comedy.

jokes.text: The date palm/date fruit tangent: 'Unlike your date palms, they come from dates. Different kind of... well, you know?' 'Yeah.' 'You've had a date, haven't you?' 'I mean the fruit.' 'Right.' 'Well, that's where it grows from.' 'What?' 'From the seed in the date.' 'The palm does?'
jokes.setup: Larry and Artie discuss palm trees while Artie moves his plant
jokes.punchline: An extended, genuine confusion about whether 'date' refers to the social event or the fruit, culminating in Larry's apparently sincere disbelief that palms grow from date seeds
jokes.explanation: This is a delightful piece of naturalistic comedy — a genuine tangent about botanical nomenclature that goes nowhere and perfectly captures how conversations actually drift. 'You've had a date, haven't you? I mean the fruit.' is a subtle jab at Larry's social life, and Larry's genuine confusion about plant reproduction is a nice bit of anti-intellectual character work.

jokes.text: Mid-plant-discussion, Hank appears and tells Regis he's in on the sidekick offer — completely derailing the botanical conversation
jokes.setup: Artie and Larry are in an absurd date palm tangent; the scene has completely lost track of the Hank situation
jokes.punchline: Hank appears with total emotional commitment: 'I've been thinking a lot about the job offer and I just want to tell you I'm in.' — interrupting a conversation about fruit seeds
jokes.explanation: The comedic whiplash of transitioning from the date palm tangent directly into Hank's big moment is very Larry Sanders Show in its rhythm — real conversations don't have clean transitions, and important moments land in the middle of trivial ones.

jokes.text: Regis: 'We're gonna start in the fall of '97.' Hank: 'What'd you say?' '...in the fall of '97.' 'But I... when are you leaving the morning show?' 'When my contract expires, which is in the fall of '97.' 'Um, but you're not quitting the show now?' 'No. What, are you nuts, Hank?'
jokes.setup: Hank has just dramatically committed to being Regis's sidekick and begins celebrating
jokes.punchline: The show doesn't start for three years — Hank quit a good job for a show that won't exist until 1997. He's ruined his life for nothing yet.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's structural punchline — everything Hank has done, quit a job, fought with Artie, strained his marriage, was predicated on a show that doesn't start for three years. The reveal is perfectly timed and structurally elegant: Regis's casual 'fall of '97' detonates quietly, then Hank's dawning horror plays out through increasingly desperate clarifying questions. 'What, are you nuts, Hank?' from Regis is the perfect cherry. This is exceptional plot-level comedy.

jokes.text: Hank, shell-shocked, asks Regis: 'Does Joyce ever give you career advice?' Regis: 'No, no. Never.' [long pause] — Hank staring into the middle distance
jokes.setup: Hank has just realized he destroyed his career over a show three years away while his wife pushed him into it
jokes.punchline: The question about Joyce giving Regis career advice is an indirect, devastated acknowledgment that Margaret has ruined him; Regis's 'Never' is the knife
jokes.explanation: The emotional precision here is extraordinary. Hank asking if Joyce gives Regis career advice — and Regis's breezy 'Never' — is the episode's most resonant moment. It's funny and sad simultaneously, which is the show's highest register. The subtext (Hank realizing his wife destroyed his career while Regis's doesn't interfere) is total, and the reaction beat that follows (Hank staring, then Artie's 'Jesus Christ, Hank!') earns every emotional beat.

jokes.text: Does Joyce ever give you career advice? No, no. Never.
jokes.setup: Hank, having just been destroyed by wife-driven career decisions, asks Regis if Joyce gives career advice
jokes.punchline: Regis's breezy, completely uncomplicated 'No, no. Never.' — the contrast with Hank's situation is the joke
jokes.explanation: The juxtaposition is precise: Hank has just destroyed his professional life because of his wife's career ambitions, and Regis (his comparison point throughout the episode) is totally free of this dynamic. 'No, no. Never.' is the kind of answer that would make Hank want to cry.

jokes.text: Artie walks in on the aftermath: 'Jesus Christ, Hank!' followed by 'Oh, my baby!' — apparently rushing to protect his plant
jokes.setup: Artie sees Hank in some kind of distressed state after the '97 revelation
jokes.punchline: Artie's cry of 'Jesus Christ, Hank!' is followed immediately by 'Oh, my baby!' — revealing his second cry is for the plant, not Hank
jokes.explanation: The plant running gag pays off brilliantly here. 'Jesus Christ, Hank!' sounds like concern for a human being, but 'Oh, my baby!' immediately reveals Artie's actual priority is the plant. The structural joke is that Artie's compassion is extended to plant life, not to Hank's crisis. The payoff of a running gag at an emotionally charged moment is perfect comedy architecture.

jokes.text: On-air Bobcat interview: Larry brings up the Tonight Show despite Bobcat explicitly saying he didn't want to discuss it due to legal reasons. Bobcat: 'I distinctly said I didn't want to.'
jokes.setup: Bobcat told Larry pre-show he couldn't discuss the Tonight Show for legal reasons; Larry acknowledged it
jokes.punchline: On air, Larry immediately brings it up anyway — the professional betrayal is instant and complete
jokes.explanation: The callback to the pre-interview agreement is perfectly constructed. Larry's betrayal — bringing up the exact thing Bobcat said not to bring up — is both funny and character-illuminating. Larry's need to have 'interesting television' overrides his promises. 'I distinctly said I didn't want to' is Bobcat's perfect exasperated response. This is the show at its most meta-savvy about talk show conventions.

jokes.text: Bobcat on air: 'Here, go crazy, go nuts! Dance for us, monkey boy! Dance!' — then apparently goes physical/wild on set
jokes.setup: Larry pushes Bobcat to explain the Tonight Show stunt even though Bobcat has legal reasons not to
jokes.punchline: Bobcat snaps and calls out the exploitative nature of booking 'dangerous' guests — then apparently demonstrates it by going physically wild
jokes.explanation: Bobcat's 'Dance for us, monkey boy! Dance!' is a remarkable piece of meta-comedy — he's articulating what Larry (and all talk show hosts) are doing when they book 'kooky' guests: exploiting chaos for entertainment. Then he demonstrates by providing the chaos. It's self-aware and subversive simultaneously. The line itself is highly quotable and conceptually sharp.

jokes.text: Larry: 'This is usually when they go to a commercial.' — delivered directly to camera or to the room as the chaos continues
jokes.setup: Bobcat has just gone physically wild on the set after his 'monkey boy' speech
jokes.punchline: 'This is usually when they go to a commercial' — Larry's reflexive resort to TV convention in the middle of real chaos
jokes.explanation: Six words that contain an entire philosophy of live television: when things go wrong, you go to commercial. Larry's calm deployment of this procedural knowledge in the middle of a meltdown is perfectly Larry — his instinct is always to manage the show, not the moment. Highly quotable, meta-textually rich.

jokes.text: Old man in wheelchair after Bobcat's chaos: 'One minute I'm standing behind the curtain eating a mint, the next thing I know I got a cardboard mountain up my ass.'
jokes.setup: Bobcat's physical chaos has apparently injured a bystander — an elderly man in a wheelchair
jokes.punchline: 'A cardboard mountain up my ass' — delivered with elderly outrage by someone who has no idea why this is happening
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best surprise jokes. The old man in the wheelchair is introduced as collateral damage from Bobcat's chaos, and 'a cardboard mountain up my ass' is a sensational description. 'One minute I'm standing behind the curtain eating a mint' is the perfect mundane setup for the absurdity of what followed. Entirely unexpected, physically funny, and the old man's authority adds gravitas to the chaos.

jokes.text: Old man: 'You young people don't know what funny is. Eddie Cantor was funny. If I didn't have arthritis, I'd knock you right on your ass.'
jokes.setup: The old man is confronting Bobcat about his comedy methods
jokes.punchline: 'If I didn't have arthritis, I'd knock you right on your ass.' — an elderly man threatening violence while defending the legacy of Eddie Cantor
jokes.explanation: The old man threatening violence while citing arthritis as the only obstacle is perfectly executed. 'Eddie Cantor was funny' as a critique of modern comedy is both funny and oddly moving — it positions the old man as a keeper of real comedy history. The frustrated violence ('I'd knock you right on your ass') from someone in a wheelchair is beautifully dark. One of the episode's best surprise performances.

jokes.text: Artie escorting Bobcat out: 'I'll escort you to your dressing room in case you get the urge to push a coke machine over on Michael Bolton.' Bobcat: 'I wouldn't do it if it wasn't televised.'
jokes.setup: Artie takes control of Bobcat after the chaos
jokes.punchline: 'I wouldn't do it if it wasn't televised.' — Bobcat's admission that his chaos is performative and media-dependent
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional. 'I wouldn't do it if it wasn't televised' is a profound piece of comedy about the relationship between performer and media — and it's delivered as a throwaway line by Bobcat. It anticipates reality TV culture, media performance, and the nature of spectacle with a single sentence. It's also deeply character-specific: Bobcat's chaos is calculated, not genuine, which is funnier and darker than if it were sincere. One of the episode's best lines by a significant margin.

jokes.text: Hank's breakdown to Larry: 'Well, bottom line is, I'm just... I'm... I'm... I'm a fucking mess. My marriage... my marriage is, uh... my life... my life is a fuckin' mess.'
jokes.setup: Hank has been through the full arc: job offers, quitting, Regis's '97 revelation, existential collapse
jokes.punchline: 'I'm a fucking mess' — the entire episode's Hank subplot collapses into this perfectly honest self-assessment
jokes.explanation: The comedy of Hank's breakdown is that it's simultaneously funny and genuinely pathetic — which is Tambor's specialty. The stumbling, repetitive sentence structure ('I'm... I'm... I'm... I'm a fucking mess') is beautifully performed, and 'my life... my life is a fucking mess' has the rhythm of a man discovering something true about himself in real time. Larry's response — 'Fine. This is fine.' — is the next joke.

jokes.text: Larry's resolution with Hank: 'Fine. This is fine.' / Hank: 'What do you mean it's fine?' / Larry: 'You mean I can stay? Yeah. Stay?' / 'Really?' / 'Yeah. See you tomorrow?' / 'S-see you tomorrow.' / 'Great. Little smile?' / 'OK. Good.'
jokes.setup: Hank has delivered an emotional breakdown; Larry receives it with minimal investment
jokes.punchline: 'Little smile? OK. Good.' — Larry's management of Hank's emotional crisis is reduced to requesting a performative smile, which Hank provides
jokes.explanation: The resolution of Hank's crisis is Larry asking for 'a little smile' — reducing all of Hank's genuine distress to a performance request. This is perfectly Larry: he doesn't solve problems, he manages optics. 'Little smile? OK. Good.' is a quietly devastating summary of their entire relationship. The comedy and the sadness are inseparable.

jokes.text: Little smile? / OK. Good.
jokes.setup: Hank has been told he can stay. He asks for a little smile from Larry.
jokes.punchline: Larry gives the minimum viable smile upon request. Hank has to solicit emotional validation from his boss like a child asking for approval.
jokes.explanation: 'Little smile?' is both heartbreaking and funny. Hank needing to explicitly request a facial expression from Larry — and Larry complying with 'OK' as if filling in a form — captures their entire relationship. The negotiated smile is Hank's reward for a day of catastrophic self-destruction.

jokes.text: Larry tells Artie to rehire Hank; Artie reveals he didn't know Hank had quit. Larry: 'Well, I'd like to know if someone quits.' Artie: 'Well, you told me you didn't want to know.'
jokes.setup: Larry tells Artie Hank is staying; Artie confirms with 'I'll bet he is' and reveals he found out about the Regis '97 situation
jokes.punchline: Larry learns Hank quit that morning — something he didn't know — and protests he should have been told; Artie points out Larry specifically said he didn't want to know
jokes.explanation: The callback to the earlier 'don't tell me how you handle it' exchange is structurally perfect. Larry demanded to not know details, Artie complied, and now Larry is complaining he wasn't informed. The irony is total and character-specific: Larry wants plausible deniability AND full information, simultaneously. Artie's flat 'Well, you told me you didn't want to know' is the perfect rejoinder. This is the show's meta-commentary on television management at its best.

jokes.text: Artie describes handling Hank: 'I called the fucker in your office here. And I told him he was pussy-whipped and he better get—' Larry: 'OK, fine, fine, fine. As long as you handled it.'
jokes.setup: Larry asks how Artie 'handled' the Hank situation; Artie begins explaining
jokes.punchline: The handling involved calling Hank pussy-whipped (which caused him to quit), but Larry cuts off the explanation — re-enacting his earlier preference not to know — even as Artie tries to tell him the full, disastrous story
jokes.explanation: The structural elegance is remarkable: Artie begins explaining that 'handling it' involved causing the crisis, but Larry cuts him off with the exact same 'as long as you handled it' from before. The show has constructed a perfect loop where Larry's management style ensures he will never know what's happening around him. The irony is complete and the character work is flawless.

jokes.text: Regis in the hallway: '2 years to get on the show, 2 years in the hallway. Ha ha ha.'
jokes.setup: Regis pops in to say goodbye after the show
jokes.punchline: He does his signature self-deprecating laugh about the wait time between booking and appearance being equivalent to the hallway time
jokes.explanation: Regis doing his self-deprecating showbiz shtick. Functional and charming but not exceptional comedy writing — it's more of a character moment that confirms Regis as the professionally cheerful insider.

jokes.text: 2 years to get on the show, 2 years in the hallway. Ha ha ha.
jokes.setup: Regis pokes his head in for a farewell. He's been made to wait in the hallway before getting on the show.
jokes.punchline: The specific math of Regis's treatment — 2 years pursuing, 2 years waiting in the corridor — delivered as cheerful self-deprecation by one of TV's biggest stars.
jokes.explanation: A nice insider-showbiz joke — even Regis Philbin has to wait in the hallway at The Larry Sanders Show. The self-deprecating cheerfulness is good Regis character work.

jokes.text: Artie's parting shot to Regis: 'But I'd tell Kathie Lee to stay about 10 feet back. OK? That's a little tip.'
jokes.setup: Artie has just assured Regis that Bobcat will be a good boy on his show
jokes.punchline: Immediately after the reassurance, Artie advises keeping Kathie Lee at a safe distance — which given the vomit plan, is an enormous understatement
jokes.explanation: This is the payoff joke for the Bobcat vomit plan established earlier. '10 feet back' as the only protection against projectile vomiting is a magnificently understated warning. Artie knows everything and tells Regis just enough to set up his own doom. The dramatic irony is total — the audience knows the full plan, Regis doesn't. Artie's 'That's a little tip' with perfect equanimity is the episode's last great character beat.

jokes.text: Episode closes on the chaos of Bobcat apparently having done something more, staff panic, producer saying: 'You know, this is gonna be all over the press in the morning. How's that gonna make us look?'
jokes.setup: Post-Bobcat chaos aftermath; someone is apologizing
jokes.punchline: The concern is not for the injured party but for press coverage and the show's image — a perfect showbiz values inversion
jokes.explanation: A solid closing irony — the showbiz world's first concern is always optics. Not exceptional but a clean thematic button on the episode's showbiz satire.

tmdb_overview: Regis Philbin causes some major unrest when he intimates to Hank that there might be place for him on Regis' new show. Larry and Artie worry about what guest Bobcat Goldthwait might do to top his chair-burning incident on The Tonight Show.
